newsitem.title: UK: NatWest loss recalls past trading upsets elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: NatWest loss recalls past trading upsets elsewhere.

text.p: The 50 million sterling ($81.2 million) provision that Britain's National Westminster Bank has had to make after finding trader mispricing errors reminded the market of past trading scandals and upsets, although it was nowhere near on the same scale.
Following are some companies and institutions which have suffered heavy losses from the activities of traders in recent years, starting with the most recent casualty, National Westminster Bank.

1997 ****February 28, National Westminster Bank, one of Britain's largest, makes a 50 million sterling provision to cover mispricing errors in the interest rate options book of its NatWest Markets unit.

A senior trader was suspended for failure to supervise and a second trader, who resigned from NatWest before the errors had been discovered, was reported to the Securities & Futures Authority (SFA) regulator.

1996 ****June 13, The world's biggest copper merchant, Sumitomo Corp, said it lost an estimated $1.8 billion over 10 years from unauthorised copper trades, primarily by chief copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
Sumitomo said it had fired Hamanaka, once dubbed "Mr Five Percent" because his trading team was believed to control five percent of the world's copper trade.

****September, Daiwa Bank, Japan's fifth largest, suffered a $1.1 billion loss from unauthorised bond trading by Toshihide Iguchi, one of its executives in the United States. U.S. authorities ordered Daiwa to close down its U.S. operations.

****February 26, British investment bank Barings Plc placed under administration after a single Singapore trader, Nick Leeson, lost more than 500 million pounds ($790 milion) in derivatives trading. Leeson was sentenced to six-and-half years in jail in Singapore in December on two counts of cheating. Barings was subsequently to Dutch bank ING.

****July, The Common Fund of the United States, which oversees almost $20 billion of funds for colleges and other educational institutions, said a rogue trader had caused it to lose about $128 million.

****December, Orange County, California, declared bankruptcy after disclosing investment losses estimated at more than US$1.6 billion from its investment portfolio, which relied heavily on derivatives.
****January, Chile Copper Corp, the world's largest copper producer better known as Codelco, lost $175 million in a financial scandal that rocked Chile.

****April, Wall Street brokerage Kidder, Peabody fired the head of its government trading desk, Joseph Jett, after the firm uncovered a scheme that created phantom trades, resulting in a one-time charge of $210 million after tax.
****December, German industrial group Metallgesellschaft suffered spectacular losses on energy products-linked derivatives, forcing creditors to mount a $2.2 billion rescue.
****April, Indian banks and brokers were accused of colluding illegally to siphon $1.3 billion from the inter-bank securities market to fuel a boom on the Bombay Stock Exchange.

****November, Michael Milken, known as the junk bond king as head of bond operations at Drexel Burnham Lambert, sentenced to 10 years in jail for securi ties fraud. Drexel filed for bankruptcy after being fined $650 million in fines and restitution.

****September, Two top officers of Italy's largest commercial bank, Banca Nazionale del Lavoro resigned because of a scandal over massive unauthorised lending to Iraq by a branch of the bank in Atlanta, Georgia. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds Sterling)
